papers.title: Rank-size analysis of optimal portfolio weights with a reverse-engineering application
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the shape of optimal portfolio weights using rank-size analysis. We consider four portfolio selection models: Global Minimum-Variance (GMV), minimum-CVaR, Risk Parity (RP), and the Most Diversified Portfolio (MDP). For each model, we fit seven rank-size specifications to the sorted portfolio weights generated over rolling windows. To compare the fitted specifications, we combine standard goodness-of-fit measures with Cumulative Second-order $\varepsilon$-Stochastic Dominance, an $\varepsilon$-parameterized generalization of Second-order Stochastic Dominance that quantifies the extent to which the exact dominance conditions are satisfied or violated. Empirically applied to major equity indices, this approach provides a systematic criterion for identifying the optimal functional form across diverse market compositions. Furthermore, we address the inverse problem of identifying the generating model from the observed weight structure. We use the calibrated rank-size parameters as inputs to a Random Forest classifier, evaluated by a blocked cross-validation that accounts for the overlap between estimation windows. The parameters separate minimum-risk from risk-diversification strategies and identify the RP and MDP portfolios, whereas the GMV and minimum-CVaR portfolios are difficult to distinguish. These results indicate that rank-size parameters provide a compact and informative description of portfolio allocation geometries.

papers.title: Portfolio Allocation under Heterogeneous Scales and Multifractality
papers.abstract: Cross-correlations between financial signals are neither scale-free nor amplitude-independent: they vary with the time scale over which they are measured and with the magnitude of the fluctuations that dominate the average. We exploit this structure to construct a portfolio allocation model in which the risk functional is the signed fluctuation function of multifractal cross-correlation analysis (MFCCA), indexed by a scale $s$ and a fluctuation order $q$. Unlike MFDCCA-type criteria, which rectify local detrended covariances before aggregation, MFCCA retains their sign, so that co-moving and counter-moving components contribute to risk with opposite signs; for $q=2$ the resulting quadratic form coincides with the detrended fluctuation function of the portfolio series itself, recovering the mean--variance criterion as a scale-dependent limit. Using two-component ARFIMA and Markov-switching multifractal processes, we show that prescribed multiscale and multifractal dependence is transmitted into the optimal weights, and that sign preservation contributes more to the reduction of tail risk than aggregation over fluctuation orders. Applied to financial multi-assets, the criterion lowers drawdown, Value-at-Risk, and expected shortfall relative to the mean--variance benchmark at every required return, in and out of sample, without any loss in realized portfolio return. The construction maps signed multiscale interaction structures onto resource-allocation decisions, which is applicable to complex financial systems whose components interact across heterogeneous scales with amplitude-dependent coupling.

papers.title: Cleaning correlation matrices with external information: the Maximum Variance estimator
papers.abstract: Rotationally invariant estimators clean the eigenvalues of an empirical correlation matrix but keep its noisy eigenvectors. We study an estimator that corrects the eigenvectors by using external information, namely a partition of the assets into groups such as asset classes or regions. The Maximum Variance (MaxVar) estimator restricts the leading eigenvectors to linear combinations of the maximum-variance portfolios of the groups and replaces the rest of the spectrum by a single eigenvalue. It is a factor model with about n parameters instead of n2/2, and it is positive de nite even when the number of observations is smaller than the number of assets n. We apply it to the correlation matrix of 47 futures on stock indices, bonds and currencies, with the three asset classes as groups. In an illustrative Monte Carlo test, in which the reference matrix has the structure assumed by the estimator, the distance to the reference is reduced by one third with respect to the empirical matrix, against less than 10% for the rotationally invariant estimator. The decisive test is the performance of a portfolio on real data: over 1993-2018, the Sharpe ratio of the risk parity portfolio, which involves the inverse of the matrix, is 1.28 with the MaxVar estimator, 1.24 with the rotationally invariant estimator and 1.17 with the empirical matrix, and the advantage increases when the estimation window is shortened.
